entries.content:
I often like John Early’s work. I love John Early’s taste. I came to one of my favorite movies, the bracing, pensive 1990 Canadian docudrama Strangers in Good Company, after he hosted a screening of it at New York’s Metrograph in 2021. On both TV and film, he’s regularly cast as frustrated and venal divas on the verge of collapse: the high-strung theater kid Logan in Wet Hot American Summer: First Day of Camp, or Jerome, Jenna Maroney’s son via long-ago egg donation on 30 Rock. This particular type reached its acme in Early’s most fully realized role, Elliott Goss on TBS’s Search Party. Goss is a malignant, cancer-faking accomplice to murder who reinvents himself as a homophobic right-wing talking head and frequently resorts to banal therapy-speak to avoid (in no particular order) work, justice, accountability, difficult conversations, professional deadlines, personal responsibility, and the basic social needs of other people. He will contort himself impossibly to deflect even the smallest amount of square, head-on honesty. Early plays dishonesty magnificently, although he has typically focused on the dishonest and venomous, not the dishonest and kind.

Which brings us to Early’s first feature-length movie, Maddie’s Secret. In July I attended a screening primarily for a chance to see, in the supporting cast, the leads (Emily Allan, Leah Hennessey, and Ruby McCollister) of the remarkable 2013 web series “Zhe Zhe,” which followed bandmates Mona DeLiza, Jean D’Arc, and Chewie Swindleburne as they pursued glamour, pain, fame, and revenge. A representative episode description declares: “Rest and relaxation are not in the cards for Mona as she suffers a mysterious illness”; a representative line, delivered dully by Jean, moments after being stabbed, to a hysterical Mona: “You’ve got local vomit all over your angora.” Regrettably, there is no line in Maddie’s Secret anywhere near as striking. It is rarely more than gently funny.

I like the way Early displays his influences openly, like an auctioneer at an estate sale: here is a shot from Douglas Sirk, here is a scene from Showgirls, here is Fly by Jing chili crisp. In Maddie’s Secret, Allan, Hennessey, and McCollister play a trio of bad girls with eating disorders opposite Early’s good girl with an eating disorder. At the plot level the film follows its source material, the 1986 bulimia melodrama Kate’s Secret, quite faithfully, and its stagey quality is recognizable to anyone familiar with Seventies- and Eighties-era after-school specials. It does not, however, precisely parody the style of Very Special TV episodes, unlike, say, The Brady Bunch Movie (1995), which might otherwise be Maddie’s Secret’s closest spiritual relative. The Brady Bunch Movie uses the exact visual grammar of the original sitcom, as well as its hokey, aw-shucks tone and earnest plotting to get its satire across. It’s both a sarcastic rendition of the corny, flat style of the old show and a loving mockery of its foursquare values. But Early seems to be making a very personal film with a lovely, distinctly Sirk-inflected aesthetic that is nevertheless somewhat at odds with the story being told.

Maddie Ralph is an ingenue dishwasher turned online influencer who is given the opportunity—spoken with the same whispered, urgent excitement as a member of Heaven’s Gate scanning the skies for the arrival of Comet Hale-Bopp—to become a food stylist for a TV show called The Boar. Like all ingenues, she is blonde and has precisely two enemies, a work rival and, of course, her mother, but is otherwise beloved by all. She is particularly beloved by her lesbian best friend, Deena (played by Kate Berlant as a sort of comic shark—Deena’s jaws snap ceaselessly, as though she is always chewing gum; whenever her eyes have the opportunity to roll, they do), and her dim, adoring husband, Jake. Jake is played by Eric Rahill as a sort of simple child; motivated by affection and hunger, easily outmaneuvered, he always seems to be on the verge of saying, “Look at what I can do!” before attempting a somersault.

Every time Maddie takes another step closer to her dream, her eating disorder escalates, as does her need to guard her privacy from those who love her most. After she collapses at an exercise class, her doctor informs her that she’s courting death and she enters inpatient treatment. Her roommate, Julie, played by a charmingly glassy-eyed Vanessa Bayer, is a naif who can seemingly do nothing but smile vacantly and attempt to secretly perform crunches when the staff are not looking. When Maddie escapes (in order to make her final interview for the Boar job, serving a home-cooked meal to the show’s producers), Julie takes her friend’s rule-breaking as tacit permission to relapse too, twisting doggedly back and forth in bed, counting all the way up to nine before the film cuts to news of her death. After this sacrificial loss, Maddie can at last “really” commit to her treatment, and she rapidly moves through the remaining beats of the rehab plot: she is now socially accepted by the previously standoffish veteran patients, cries at the expected moments during a therapy session with her wicked mother (Kristen Johnston, who is tremendous), produces a legible origin story that allows the staff to permit her to graduate, and returns home.

Advertisement

Jake might be described in modern online parlance as “an eater,” someone who readily telegraphs a mighty appetite for pussy and food. He openly lusts after Maddie (although he stops just short of offensive perversion), eats whatever she cooks with obvious relish, and instinctively shuts down her self-deprecating comments, seeing no faults in either her body or her cooking. He is beautifully paradigmatic of the oblivious partner of someone with an eating disorder: he can be easily dismissed and lied to without guilt, since he’s too unobservant or stupid to realize he ought to hate her, as she hates herself.

And Maddie’s secret, or at least one of them, is that she also hates her husband (although she will never relinquish her compulsive affect of warmth toward him), not least for refusing to treat her with the sort of operatic cruelty that her mother does. On multiple occasions, when backed into a corner, she tells him that she is pregnant rather than disclose her bulimia relapse(s); the more excited he gets about the idea, the more disgusted and dispirited she becomes with it, and with him.

A great deal of the critical reception to Maddie’s Secret has, somewhat oddly, praised the film for its earnestness. The headline for IndieWire’s review is “John Early’s Directorial Debut Comedy Is More Sincere Than Satirical,” while The Film Stage calls it a “sincere satire.” I suspect, although I cannot be sure, that what people mean when they call this movie sincere is something between “I found John Early’s drag to be effective and consistent” and “I do not think this movie is trying to make fun of people with eating disorders,” both of which are certainly true.

But Maddie is a woman incapable of speaking sincerely, who refuses honesty at every turn, who stages a phony breakdown/recommitment to “the process” in order to sneak out of rehab for a job interview, who never admits to anything. I think Early likes ingenues and wanted to play one, and he does a creditable job; if anything, I found Berlant’s drag as a butch lothario false and off-putting. Her every gesture, every line, hits a cartoonish note. I was sorry to see a diva so miscast in bad wolf drag. It was the most I have ever disliked her onscreen, and I normally find her a great deal of fun to watch.

Maddie is literally tight-lipped. The audience might rightfully anticipate a burst of, if not vomit, repressed cathartic speech at some point in the rehabilitation plot, but Early presents us with a heroine who cannot or will not be evacuated. Maddie does not behave sincerely, but she is bombarded with sincerity—sincere admiration, sincere concern, sincere therapeutic treatment, sincere abuse—and is in fact scarcely able to survive it.

This instinctive retreat from intimacy exists in all directions. In another movie, the problem of Maddie’s horrified discomfort at the prospect of experiencing support, care, and desire from her loving husband would be solved by Deena’s obvious romantic overtures; Jake could easily be turned into a truly bad husband so that the audience could celebrate a lesbian cuckolding. But in Maddie’s Secret Deena’s subplot is moved further and further from the film’s center once Maddie befriends her fellows in rehab. Deena eventually gets herself admitted to the ward by faking an eating disorder of her own, after which Maddie reveals that she has reported her to the hospital administration (offscreen), and blankly watches Deena break down as she is transferred to a different psychiatric unit. Maddie goes from being superficially unconscious of Deena’s sexual interest to coldly rejecting, pitying, and denying it, insisting in her sweet condescension that their separation and Deena’s subsequent detention is for the best. Nothing could be more sincere than Deena’s desire for Maddie. Nothing but sincerity could horrify Maddie into not just rejecting her but seeing to her incarceration.

When it comes to onscreen representations of vomiting, the trend in the last forty years (from Stand by Me to Triangle of Sadness) has been toward the explicit and the detailed, but Maddie’s Secret remains, like its heroine, conspicuously discreet; bulimic episodes are signaled by shots of Maddie tying her hair into a ponytail with grim determination before the camera tastefully pans away. On the other hand, most scenes involving food consumption are quite explicitly off-putting. The camera lingers on sheens of grease and stray crumbs, while sounds of slurping, belching, chewing, and rumbling are magnified tenfold.

Advertisement

Maddie’s Secret does, I think, rely on the earnestness of the midcentury melodrama in the same way that Airplane! relies on the earnestness of Zero Hour, but it does not produce any new earnestness of its own. There’s a real interest in revulsion, in nausea, in messiness, escalation, and the post-binge climactic clarity of self-disgust, but a remarkable resistance to catharsis. The film is less concerned with “fixing” its ingenue than in mourning her absence—as a vehicle for melodrama, kitsch, and drag—from the contemporary star-making system: today’s ingenue does not receive a starring role in a romantic drama with a $40 million budget; she eats a burrito in her car while a friend films her exaggerating a cheese pull, in the hopes that she can be a food stylist for a middlebrow television show. What are we going to do with actresses if we don’t give them films to live on? They’ll eat themselves, they’ll break down like plastic bottles in a landfill, they’ll self-digest, they’ll get fractured as they stay big and the screens get smaller.

The closest the movie gets to offering a moment of disclosure comes during a forced joint-therapy session between Maddie and her monstrous mother, during which Maddie haltingly recites a litany of sexual, physical, and psychological abuse inflicted upon her as a child. But the monologue is cut jarringly short (“Careful, Maddie, you’re hurting my knee,” her mother says, halfway between alarmed and contemptuous, jumping up to leave with the admission that “this is all I can do for today”), and the emphasis remains on narrative rather than on feeling. This particular encounter must take place because it is at this point in the rehab plot that the heroine must confess and cry in front of her therapist, and while it is certainly believable that Maddie has been thoroughly abused by her mother, it never seems like the start of a new basis for living. “I never needed the love of a father,” Maddie cries right before her mother leaves. “I needed your love, Mommy.” But both Maddie and the audience were already perfectly aware that Maddie is desperate for love, affirmation, and praise. If anything, her vulnerability and fragility have been her most effective weapons in the fight against self-awareness; for clarity to even possibly produce something like change for her, it would have to look very different from “I need love.”

Like Maddie herself, Maddie’s Secret is motivated by evasiveness. The film itself often lurches away from possible plot developments, usually at the last moment. (One of the many comforts of bulimia is that it always provides its sufferer with the opportunity to change her mind. Go ahead and eat dinner now! You can always take it back later.) A timid conversation between Maddie and Jake at the very end of the movie—a scene that may suggest he is moving out, or may not—confirms that she will not break down, nor admit to anything true:

“How do I know you’re telling the truth?” he asks, referring to her insistence that she hasn’t had a setback.

A deep inhale, a shaky look at the middle distance, a small smile that grows in self-assurance—Early is a master interpreter of the ingenue’s catalog of gestures—“I guess you don’t.” There will be no new era of openness between them.

Once the secret of an eating disorder is made public, sincerity in the form of concern and pressure and observation is brought to bear upon the subject until she offers up an emotional disclosure. Until this disclosure is purged, she has no hope of being left alone. (Early has discussed elsewhere his own experience growing up as an evangelical Christian in the American South, a culture where frequent public confessions are prized, the more frequent and the more debasing the greater the social reward.) Maddie’s greatest and most cherished secret is that she wants to have nothing to say, and no one is going to take that from her.

entries.title: From the Horse’s Mouth
entries.summary: “Punwise, I didn’t feel too reined in on BoJack. If I was champing at the bit to use a joke somewhere, I could usually find a place to trot it out!”
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
This article is part of a regular series of conversations with the Review’s contributors; read past entries here and sign up for our email newsletter to get them delivered to your inbox each week.

In 2013, shortly after I gave birth to my daughter, the Canadian publisher Drawn and Quarterly sent me a copy of My Dirty Dumb Eyes, by Lisa Hanawalt. Her art and writing made me laugh out loud through the mire of postpartum depression, and I’ve been a devoted fan ever since. So this June I direct-messaged her to ask if she might draw the cover for our Summer Issue; to my delight, she accepted. In an early sketch, Hanawalt included some made-up coverlines, which I wished were real: Jessipa Jonesky: Talking to Ghosts at the Local Diner; Allain St. Brewing: Donkeys, Doorknobs, and Dubrivnik; Chilm Timbers: Where Did I Put My Car Keys?; Cindy Chomps: Ballet on the Playground; Santiago Biggle: Kafka’s Lost Poems; Bageta Suzsmith: Trick-or-Treat in Outerspace; Verily Spivak: I’m Too Cold to Go Swimming; Omar Meerkowtow: High School Dances and Broadway Revivals.

Hanawalt’s genius, I think, is in her evocation of the bodily and disembodied absurdities of being human and animal at the same time. She is best known as the creator of the television series BoJack Horseman (2014–2020), about a depressed horse-man, which Adam Thirlwell called, enthusiastically, “an opioid version” of Ibsen in our August 20, 2020, issue. She followed BoJack with the series Tuca and Bertie (2019–2022), which makes my now teenage daughter crack up. In addition to My Dumb Dirty Eyes, Hanawalt has also written and illustrated the books Hot Dog Taste Test (2016) and Coyote Doggirl (2018), and she illustrated the children’s book Benny’s Brigade (2012).

Hanawalt lives in Los Angeles, where she rides her horse, Juniper. Her graphic memoir, I Can’t Stop Thinking About Horses and Sex, will publish in October. I wrote to her last month to ask about writing, her childhood, and her sense of humor.

Leanne Shapton: What were you like as a child? What did you grow up looking at?

Lisa Hanawalt: I was always daydreaming and drawing during class, fully embodied in my fursonas at all times, afraid to shit, shy, hyper, tomboyish, and crushing on boys. I grew up looking at Bambi, Garfield, Lisa Simpson, and the Guns N’ Roses music video for “November Rain.”

Do you write as much as you draw, or do they happen simultaneously?

I think it’s an even, fifty-fifty split, but I am more confident drawing. With writing, I never quite feel like I’m nailing it.

It’s crazy to hear you say you don’t think you nail your writing. You’re so adept at folly and phrasing and dialogue. What are some books you’ve been reading or rereading?

I’ve been having an attack of bad attention span (self- and Meta-inflicted) and need to lock in, but I’ve been slowly reading Oscar Wilde’s The Picture of Dorian Gray, and it’s a hoot! A gothic hoot! I have also been returning to Laurie Colwin’s books, especially Happy All the Time. I just love how she writes about crabby, weird, horny women.

So where did the image on the Review’s cover come from?

I drew it in my sketchbook, lying on my couch, staring out the window at night, while watching The Truman Show.

Your writing and dialogue tend to be sophisticated and sly—unselfconsciously funny—while at the same time sincere and heartfelt. Where does your sense of humor come from?

My family is funny, I’m drawn to class clowns, and I watch and read a lot of comedy, so by osmosis I’m kinda funny too. Humor is also one of the best, least self-destructive coping mechanisms for pain and depression…not to get too serious.

What comedy have you been watching or reading? For example, I’m curious if you’ve read Tony Tulathimutte’s Rejection.

I loved Rejection so much, I drew some fan art and mailed it to Tony (I never do stuff like that). He’s the king. He also wrote the funniest “Grub Street Diet” entry ever.

Sam Irby recently wrote a blog post called “How to Stay Married” that I can’t stop thinking about.

I saw the comedian Steph Tolev open for Stavros Halkias at the Wiltern, in LA, and my face hurt from laughing, she’s so wildly lewd. Both of them were incredible.

Sandy Honig made a short film, The Weird Guy, last year that is so funny and also gorgeously shot. I also really enjoyed her episode of Caleb Hearon’s podcast So True.

I love watching the improv show Make Some Noise, on the Dropout network.

Brittani Nichols wrote a short substack post about how she doesn’t have writer’s block that made me laugh a lot. (Same here, I don’t have that.)

Is there an animal pun you never found a use for in BoJack that you’d like to put somewhere?

Advertisement

Punwise, I didn’t feel too reined in on BoJack. If I was champing at the bit to use a joke somewhere, I could usually find a place to trot it out! So, to answer your question…neight really.

What traditions (visually and verbally) do you think your work follows, if any?

Storytelling in the oldest sense, like people telling fables around a fire and drawing stuff on cave walls.

What’s your relationship with the publishers Drawn and Quarterly like?

I’ve done five books with them (including the upcoming I Can’t Stop Thinking About Sex and Horses! Out this Fall! Plug!!)—we have a lot of mutual trust and they give me a lot of creative freedom, and because we’ve signed a sacred blood bond. As a young, I didn’t pay much attention to or understand what comics publishers did, and I didn’t know their blood oath rituals required so much blood! (This is a joke, I’m joking)

I’m interested in nonverbal communication. How do you communicate with the horses in your life?

I talk to my horse, smell her breath, and scratch her back until I get manure under my nails. I feel disembodied from spending too much time on the internet, so this helps ground me and lift my mood. Her name is Juniper and I’m basically using her as an SSRI, so maybe I should have named her “Zoloft.”

entries.title: What Does a Puta Want?
entries.summary: In 1984, the year before Brazil transitioned from a military dictatorship to a tenuous democracy, a young woman named Gabriela Leite attended a national meeting for sex workers held by a progressive ministry of the Catholic Church. entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In 1984, the year before Brazil transitioned from a military dictatorship to a tenuous democracy, a young woman named Gabriela Leite attended a national meeting for sex workers held by a progressive ministry of the Catholic Church. There she shocked those assembled by taking the microphone and unabashedly calling herself a prostitute. As she recalled in her 2008 memoir, the ministry tended to use euphemisms like “girl” and “marginalized woman”—which she had come to reject. “I told the audience: ‘I think it is because people are ashamed of the word prostitute.’ That caused quite a commotion,” she wrote.

In the years that followed Leite and her colleague Lourdes Barreto, echoing a number of their peers around the world, chose to refer to themselves with the dreaded words prostituta and, especially, puta, even as “sex worker” emerged as most activists’ preferred term. Puta can mean either “whore” or “slut” in both Portuguese and Spanish; its reclamation, both in Brazil and by Spanish-speaking activists such as Georgina Orellano of Argentina, has signaled a rejection of the taboos endured not only by sex workers but by any woman who transgresses traditional sexual mores. “I’ve always liked the word,” Leite said shortly before she died of cancer in 2013. “If all putas didn’t live with so much stigma in their heads, they would use [it].”

Leite and Barreto defined their movement as a repudiation of the shame that had, for so long, discouraged prostitutes from speaking out about the abuses they suffered. Such abuse often took the form of police brutality, which Leite had begun protesting in the late 1970s. While selling sex has never been illegal in Brazil, prostitutes have long been persecuted on charges such as vagrancy and pimping, repression that intensified in the late 1970s, over a decade into Brazil’s iron-fisted military dictatorship. When two women disappeared after being loaded onto a police van in São Paulo in 1979, Leite, then a young university dropout, led a group of sex workers in staging a series of demonstrations in the city’s main square. By 1980 they had joined with gay men and travestis1 who were decrying a recent wave of arbitrary arrests in their own communities, all of them part of a broader redemocratization movement that also included feminists, trade unionists, and student activists. At protests in São Paulo, sex workers joined their queer allies in chanting a slogan that brought together the militancy of the New Left with the hedonism of the counterculture: “Abaixo a repressão, mais amor e mais tesão!” (Down with repression, more love and more desire!)

As the democratic transition progressed, Leite and other sex-worker activists organized for their rights through the Catholic Church, whose progressive clerics, inspired by the liberation theology that had taken the Latin American Church by storm in the previous decade, had begun pastoral outreach among prostitutes. Breaking with a precedent of treating women who sold sex as reprehensible deviants, they sought to understand the structural factors that shaped their decisions, such as sexism, prejudice against single mothers, and unchecked capitalism—sketching the outlines of an analysis that would later be central to the sex workers’ movement. These clerics’ rejection of the stigma against prostitution and their emphasis on prostitutes’ self-worth and dignity deeply appealed to Leite and her cohort. Yet they soon came to chafe at the Church’s paternalism: even the most left-wing clergy were staunch abolitionists, meaning that they objected on religious and moral grounds to prostitution as such. If women developed sufficient self-esteem, these priests believed, they would have the psychological wherewithal to leave the profession and opt for more respectable ones.

Through its ministries, the Church provided sex workers with the resources necessary to jumpstart their activism; in fact, it was at the 1984 meeting that Leite and Barreto first met each other and began scheming about moving out from under the clergy’s watchful eye. By the end of the 1980s they had publicly rejected its abolitionism and formed an autonomous social movement. In her memoir, published in my English translation in 2024, Leite recalls the origins of the sex-workers’ movement, including the Primeiro Encontro Nacional de Prostitutas (First National Meeting of Prostitutes) in Rio de Janeiro in 1987, where several dozen delegates from across the country discussed issues such as violence, public health, and stigma. Together they devised a platform that involved defending prostitution as a legitimate livelihood, demanding an end to police violence, and shifting public attitudes toward prostitutes and their families.

The movement, led by Leite and Barreto, went on to collaborate with the newly reconfigured Ministry of Health on accessible, non-stigmatizing HIV/AIDS prevention materials; launch an eclectic newspaper for sex workers and their allies, an impish clothing line, and numerous other cultural ventures; and lobby politicians to fully decriminalize all aspects of adult, voluntary prostitution. (The latter achievement still eludes them: third-party activities, such as owning a brothel or otherwise facilitating sexual commerce, remain criminalized in Brazil, meaning that most establishments operate underground, leaving sex workers more vulnerable to exploitation from employers and violence from clients.)

Advertisement

Over its almost fifty-year history, the Brazilian sex-workers’ movement has taken pleasure in ruffling feathers and poking fun at the pieties of the bourgeois mainstream. Barreto, for example, now an octogenarian and still an important national leader, has “Eu sou puta” (“I am a whore”) and “Vagina tem poder” (“Vagina has power”) tattooed on her forearm. The reclamation of the word “whore” was not a gesture unique to Latin America: in the 1980s a series of World Whores’ Congresses in the US and Europe produced a manifesto of sex-worker rights and staged cheeky parades and a flamboyant “Hooker’s Ball.” The irreverence and playful tone of the international movement found a good home in Brazil, the country of Carnaval, where hedonistic revelry, raucous genderbending, and freewheeling attitudes toward sex and nudity have long coexisted with traditional Catholic piety and preoccupations with female sexual honor.

Even Carol Leigh, the crimson-haired firebrand who coined the term “sex work” in 1979, was skeptical of the zeal with which it was taken up in activist circles and beyond. While the label “has been politically advantageous for us,” she wrote in her foreword to Leite’s memoir—shortly before her own death from cancer in 2022—she agreed with Leite that “we cannot forget the provocative spirit of the whore, and the power that comes from embracing the terms that have been used to stigmatize us.” Leigh recalled that Leite, whom she first met at the 1989 World Whores’ Summit in San Francisco, believed that “sex worker was thrust upon her in NGO circles to sanitize prostitution,” while “puta was a rich, evocative word with a history and a culture.” Rather than submit to a form of respectability politics, Leite, Barreto, and other Brazilian activists retained and relished what Leigh called their “whore’s-eye view.”

So what is a puta, and what does she want? Like her whore sisters to the North, she embraces deviance and provocation while also making pointed critiques of patriarchy, capitalism, empty moralism, and US hegemony. In the last decade, this venerable tradition of puta organizing has given rise to what the Brazilian activist and sex worker Monique Prada in the 2010s named putafeminismo, or putafeminism. For reasons that are perhaps obvious, feminist and sex-worker movements have often found themselves at odds regarding questions of sexuality, agency, and empowerment. But putafeminism aims to reconcile the two, calling for a working-class, sex-radical feminism that positions whores as its flagbearers.

Thanks to a recent spate of translations, a number of these putas have reached the bookshelves and bedside tables of the Anglophone world. In addition to Duke University Press’s publication of Leite’s memoir, last year Feminist Press released Prada’s Putafeminista: A Manifesto of Sex Worker Feminism, edited and translated by Amanda De Lisio, and So What If I’m a Puta: Diaries of Transness, Sex Work, Desire, by Amara Moira, translated by De Lisio and Bruna Dantas Lobato. (Both were originally published in Brazil in 2018.) Moira and Prada, a generation younger than Leite, have emerged alongside the activist and author Indianarae Siqueira as what Prada calls a “puta trinity” at the vanguard of a new sexual politics in Latin America’s largest and most populous nation. Their writings present sex work not just as a legitimate livelihood under patriarchal capitalism but also as an opportunity to redraw the predictable lines of desire and self-determination.

Putafeminista is a call to arms, building on Prada’s longstanding advocacy for sex workers across Brazil. In 2015 she cofounded the Central Única de Trabalhadoras e Trabalhadores Sexuais (Unified Central of Sex Workers), or CUTS, a tongue-in-cheek reference to the Central Única dos Trabalhadores (CUT), Brazil’s national union federation, which emerged as a major player in national politics during the democratic transition of the 1980s—and which in 2013 refused to recognize sex work as legitimate work. Today, she is affiliated with the Articulação Nacional de Profissionais do Sexo (National Articulation of Sex Professionals), which sponsors research projects on sex work, organizes national conferences, and supports local sex-worker groups across the country.

In public appearances and on her popular blog mundoinvisível.org, Prada speaks about prostitutes primarily as workers, foregrounding their labor and material struggles: “I consider it politically important to make a clear statement that sex work is work,” she writes in Putafeminista. “Prostitution, if it cannot be considered just another form of work—a definition that would erase its specificities and issues, not only labor related but also a series of taboos, stigmas, and oppressions tied to human sexuality, especially female sexuality—has been a possible profession for a vast number of people in the place where I come from and in many places I have been.”

Advertisement

Prada has prioritized finding common cause with broader working-class movements. In the 2010s she advocated for the socialist congressman Jean Wyllys’s bill to fully legalize and regulate sex work, and she often speaks out against the growing cohort of evangelical lawmakers pushing to criminalize the profession: “Simply repressing or banning prostitution would not effectively end the stigma,” she writes in her book. “Instead of providing safety, these laws often worsen the precariousness of already vulnerable individuals, forcing women into hiding and into social isolation.”

Her fellow activist Moira—whose So What If I’m a Puta is essentially a diary of her first few years as a travesti prostitute in the state of São Paulo—is one of Brazil’s most outspoken advocates for trans rights and the full decriminalization of sex work. In recent years she has also become a public intellectual of sorts, routinely lecturing on sex-worker writing, trans rights, and depictions of queerness in literature, both in Brazil and abroad. In 2024 she published Neca, a critically acclaimed novel written in bajubá, an amalgam of Brazilian Portuguese and West African languages spoken by enslaved people that was developed by queer communities during Brazil’s military dictatorship to evade police repression, and is now a sociolect among travesti and trans women.

Rounding out the puta trinity, Indianarae Siqueira, the author of a recent memoir, Uma vida em DesTransição (A Life in DeTransition) (2024), leads Rio’s Casa Nem, a shelter and cultural center for queer and trans people. In June 2026 Siqueira announced that they were running to be a state representative on the Workers’ Party ticket, hoping for more success than Leite and Barreto—both of whom sought public office in decades past—at convincing voters to support the puta agenda. Across Brazil, in the face of a burgeoning social conservatism, these activists and many others channel the movement’s longstanding spirit of revelry, playfulness, and provocation into a serious political commitment to bettering the lives of sex workers and other sexual minorities. In recent years, groups in Rio de Janeiro and the Amazonian city of Belém do Pará have organized Carnaval floats that pay tribute to the movement’s “putriarchs,” marching through city streets and Rio’s famed Sambódromo—a stone’s throw from the location of the city’s first red-light district, Mangue—dressed in fishnet stockings and red sequined bustiers alongside giant likenesses of the whores of times past.

Leite, Prada, and Moira’s books are part of a genre of sex-worker writing that has long enjoyed critical and commercial success. Why do readers pick up any of the dozens of memoirs, manifestos, and tell-all volumes written by sex workers? Surely some hope to uncover titillating details about the sex lives of others, curious about what kind of sex men request when they pay for it, when the terms of pleasure are exclusively defined by one party in the sexual exchange. (Do they seek to please the sex worker, some may wonder, or simply enact their own fantasies, unencumbered by the interpersonal ethics, social conventions, or political convictions that in unremunerated sex may keep their more violent and domineering desires in check?) Or perhaps it is to vicariously access the presumed expertise wielded by the sex worker, that goddess of the erotic arts. By reading her words, we might just take on some of her desirability, the allure and skill that compel people to pay to take her to bed.

Some works in the genre tap into voyeuristic impulses, tending toward the confessional or even the graphic, containing little in the way of political critique. Publishers splash provocative titles on covers adorned with lithe silhouettes, strappy high heels, or voluptuous bosoms stuffed into intricate corseting—or with a coy (or not so coy) portrait of the writer herself. (The cover of Liara Roux’s Whore of New York, for example, features her reclining in bed, her ample cleavage framed by a red silk dress pulled down over one shoulder.) In Brazil, this voyeuristic tendency is best represented by the blog-turned-bestselling memoir of Bruna Surfistinha, the nom de guerre of Raquel Pacheco, a high-end escort who chronicled her sessions with clients in São Paulo in the 2000s, quickly becoming a media sensation and later the subject of a feature film.

That’s not to say that such writing has no sociological or literary appeal. The feminist porn actress and director Candida Royalle, whose artistic, literary, and flesh-bound endeavors are brilliantly memorialized in a recent biography by the historian Jane Kamensky, wrote with candor and sensitivity—as well as her characteristic coquettishness—about her work both in front of and behind the camera over a decades-long career.2 Perhaps most idiosyncratic (and beloved) in this vein is The Little Black Book of Grisélidis Réal: Days and Nights of an Anarchist Whore, in which the veteran Swiss prostitute divulges a client list complete with charmingly frank annotations. (“Alfredo: Near-dwarf Sicilian—suck, fuck, do not rush him 70 F.”)

Sex sells. Yet some sex-worker memoirs—rather than disclosing lurid details about people who could be our neighbors, colleagues, or even spouses—deploy a more defiant and less salacious tone, focusing less on the sex than on the work of the authors’ profession. Carol Leigh, aka Scarlot Harlot, the self-proclaimed “unrepentant whore” and grande dame of Bay Area sex-worker activism, was a pioneer of politicized sex-worker writing, blending a penchant for theatrical provocation and bawdy humor with hard-hitting critiques of sexism and moralism.

In recent years a younger cohort has taken up this approach even more zealously: in Revolting Prostitutes (2018), the British activists Molly Smith and Juno Mac argue for defending sex workers’ rights while remaining skeptical of the tendency, however well-intentioned, to claim that sex work is good work. They remind us that most sex workers labor in precarious if not dangerous conditions—risks that often correspond to race, gender, immigration status, and disability. In the US, the journalist and former sex worker Melissa Gira Grant has written extensively about the harms both of repressive legislation like SESTA/FOSTA, which pushes sex work underground, and of global efforts to eliminate sex trafficking, which, she argues, often lend themselves to a draconian, prohibitionist, and anti-migrant agenda that ultimately exposes workers to more violence and exploitation. Elsewhere, Charlotte Shane, who wrote the foreword to Moira’s English translation, has reflected more broadly on the often contradictory—and at times troubling—nature of desire and power in intimate relationships. Sex work, in her depiction, becomes a terrain in which practitioners and clients can work through such quandaries free from the constraining social conventions that govern noncommercial sex and dating.3

Sex-worker literature also has a rich history in Brazil, dating back to the 1980s and the founding of the Brazilian Network of Prostitutes. It now appears to be in its golden age. Barreto’s poignant and plainspoken memoir, Puta autobiografia, was published in Portuguese in 2023, joining Leite’s 1992 and 2008 volumes and the many essays and editorials that have appeared in the movement’s newspaper, Beijo da rua, since its founding in 1988. In her prolific writing, Leite championed prostitution as not only the world’s oldest profession but also one of its noblest, a sacred calling to meet people’s most profound needs for intimacy and companionship. She eulogized the prostitutes of Ancient Greece—who, in her rendering, were highly respected connoisseurs of art, philosophy, and science—and waxed poetic about the glamor and seduction of the “red lights” of prostitution zones. In addition to acting as confidantes, informal psychologists, and friends, Leite believed that prostitutes could serve as sex therapists for the handicapped, insecure, or inexperienced. In her memoir, she recalls “blind men, guys paralyzed from the waist down that couldn’t have erections but still had desire.… Not all prostitutes understand that this is a privilege of our profession, that it is one of its most noble aspects—this learned solidarity, the breaking of prejudices that are so embedded in our society, forces that worship beauty and marginalize difference.”

Prada and Moira pay homage to their puta foremothers, especially Leite, but they also challenge some of their premises. Prada in particular is unsentimental in her appraisal of contemporary prostitution, dispensing with Leite’s nostalgia for the bohemian meccas of the past and taking a much less sanguine view of the power dynamics that structure the commercial sexual marketplace. For her, the brothel is “the final frontier…where misogyny nests.” In paid sex, she writes, “women’s sexuality is often positioned to serve the desires of clients,” an arrangement that offers few opportunities to subvert entrenched gender hierarchies. Repudiating both the uncritical sex positivity of some figures in her milieu and the radical feminist conviction that prostitution is tantamount to selling an organ (“as of the last time I checked, my pussy was still intact,” she quips), she arrives at a matter-of-fact, heterodox view of sex work that makes room for ambivalence in debates long characterized by their polarizations.

Another divergence from Leite’s intellectual legacy is Prada’s unequivocal self-fashioning as a feminist, an identity of which Leite remained wary. While Leite felt snubbed and alienated by abolitionist feminists starting in the 1980s, Prada is part of a younger, iconoclastic third wave that has room for her brand of feminism—one that is “not moralistic, punitive, or victimizing”—under its big tent. For her, feminism is best represented not by orthodox radicals or intellectuals but by working women, grassroots militants who live “a raw and essential feminism necessary for their survival.”

Prada takes particular aim at what she considers the “naïve” claim that sex work is “empowering”; for her, no work under capitalism, especially precarious work, can empower the worker or wholly subvert the system. What prostitutes can and do subvert, she writes, echoing the socialist feminists of the Wages for Housework movement of the 1970s, is the logic of patriarchal capitalism that mandates and naturalizes women’s unpaid labor behind the facades of romance and family. On why women pursue sex work, Prada takes a nuanced view. She recalls how, in her own case, a capacious desire for sex prompted her to take up the profession, even as she bluntly states that most women who sell sex do so because they have to. Like Smith and Mac, her politics is, essentially, anti-work: all work under capitalism is bad, she suggests, but in certain situations sex work is the least bad option.

And even if sex work is often bad work, Prada insists, its practitioners are nonetheless entitled to more robust rights, more respect, less shame. It is partly for this reason that Prada prefers “sex worker” to other monikers. At the same time, she writes, “I like the word puta a lot,” enough to christen a movement under its banner. Putafeminism, she writes, transforms an enduring stigma into a militant pride, “strengthening our fight for rights without having to give up our work or be ashamed of it.”

Unlike Prada, Moira treats sex work as a vocation. “Giving pleasure was my bitter fate,” she writes in So What If I’m a Puta, a collection of short vignettes in the tradition of the crônica that offers a contemplative, morally ambiguous, and searching rumination on sex work and transness. “Giving, but also receiving. If getting pleasure from work is a key factor in choosing a career, then mine was already chosen.” Moira was pursuing a doctorate in literary theory at the prestigious University of Campinas when she started selling sex, meaning she came from a different class than many of her colleagues in the dark streets and squalid parking lots where they peddled their wares. She points out, however, that professional opportunities are scarce for any gender nonconforming person in Brazil, regardless of their educational qualifications or social capital. In deft prose, Moira writes unsparingly about the violence and exploitation she experienced on the job: painful and degrading sex, stealthing (non-consensual removal of a condom), shameless haggling, verbal abuse. All this dehumanizing treatment weighs on her as the narrative progresses: she speaks of hitting a “crisis point with that merciless string of bastards,” feeling “not just physical pain, but also the psychic pain of being unable to say no.”

And yet she ultimately suggests that the work offered a psychological lifeline as well as an economic one, validating her transness and allowing her to feel like a woman—which, as all women are surely aware, may involve violence and contempt alongside “admiration and desire.” Prada and Moira both first became public figures through blogs in which they divulged their exploits, and it is clear that, for Moira, writing became a way to make sense of her often bewildering and paradoxical experiences of precarity, violence, and desire. “These men paid me close to nothing for the sex I performed for them,” she writes, “but they didn’t know I was getting a story out of it too…. I was always the narrator.” Struggling to find rewarding sex and companionship in nonremunerative relationships—and aware that being with her could make her partners vulnerable to the violence and discrimination directed at trans people—she concluded that sex work afforded “the only love society had reserved for me—the only kind of love I could experience that wouldn’t put anyone else at risk.”

Unlike Prada, who tells us that she “never looked for even a shred of soul or humanity in my lovers per hour,” Moira makes a generous attempt to understand her clients’ lust and internalized prejudices, expressing sympathy for fat, brutish men, ones with hairy nipples and bad breath, society’s unwanted, who can only fulfill their desires by paying for sex. As Siqueira has said, defending the Johns so often painted as rapacious or uncaring (even sex-positive defenses of sex work don’t have much to say in favor of clients): “They’re not the soulless villains of popular imaginaries, sick, dirty losers—they are our parents, our brothers, our uncles, our children, our neighbors.”

By simultaneously offering a defense of sex work and a critique of it, putafeminism seems to offer a way past some of the most caustic divides in Anglophone feminism—those rooted in the “sex wars” that polarized the second wave in the late 1970s and 1980s. Anti-pornography radical feminists such as Catharine MacKinnon and Andrea Dworkin famously argued that commercial sex reduced women to the status of objects; in an influential 1979 book, for example, the anti-trafficking activist Kathleen Barry equated prostitution to “female sexual slavery.” Pro-sex or sex-radical feminists such as Patrick Califia, Ellen Willis, and Gayle Rubin, on the other hand, while they rarely defended conventional pornography and prostitution as good for women, believed that paid sex offered the potential for experimentation, self-expression, and liberation for men and women alike.

This sex-positive camp also argued that banning porn and sex work would ultimately serve reactionary, moralistic ends, a warning that has proved prescient. Radical-feminist arguments against legalizing sex work—including those for the so-called Nordic model, which only criminalizes clients and third parties like pimps—have indeed inadvertently contributed to the criminalization of vulnerable women by depriving them of safer, regulated workplaces while justifying crackdowns on migrants who are detained and deported for selling sex. They have also fueled a dangerous conflation of voluntary and coerced sex work. The 2018 SESTA/FOSTA legislation, for example, which was supposed to combat sex trafficking and the exploitation of minors, and was supported by the radical feminist Coalition Against Trafficking in Women, shut down online platforms that had allowed sex workers to exercise more control over their client selection and working conditions.

These debates were never really laid to rest. Radical feminists’ attempts to ban pornography now seem almost quaint, or perhaps even comical, amid the oceans of professional porn and the armies of amateur creators operating via websites such as OnlyFans. Yet in my experience teaching college students about the history of sex-worker activism, I routinely hear young people suggest that prostitution is inherently degrading or repeat sensationalized claims about the prevalence of sex trafficking. In some progressive circles, on the other hand, young women producing content for online platforms proudly proclaim themselves to be sex workers. Here the discourse of sex work as work—even good, empowering work—has taken on some of the trappings of a defanged neoliberal feminism: women as erotic entrepreneurs, girl bosses getting rich from being desired. Despite some of its more transgressive gestures—its attempts to subvert notions of female sexual propriety and challenge taboo—this posture feels unsatisfying, too, exchanging a genuinely radical politics for an indiscriminate embrace of work under capitalism and sex under patriarchy.

Like the sex radicals before them, putafeminists have little trouble accepting the premises that sex involves both pleasure and danger and that we may not always fully understand or endorse the things that turn us on. They depict sex, and even paid sex, as a terrain of struggle: a potential venue for self-expression, but also, or perhaps more importantly, a paycheck, a workplace, a means of resistance. Many of us who work for money can probably identify with the experience of having a job that is both pleasurable and burdensome, something we choose to do but that also weighs us down. And virtually everyone likely understands that any job only ever represents, at best, the least bad option in a limited array. Putafeminism is a feminism that speaks to the world as we live in it, affirming pleasure, deviance, and the complexity of desire while also foregrounding the material concerns and demands—about working conditions, violence, health, and precarity—that tend to populate the agendas of postcolonial feminists.

“I urge you to listen to a sex worker as you would to anyone else,” goes Prada’s final entreaty—yet the proposition of putafeminism is that putas have something unique to tell us. Rather than relegating sex workers to the shadowy corner that mainstream feminism reserves for anyone who bedevils its taxonomies of good and bad, putafeminists stress that the whore’s experience of sex and work gives her particular insight into the female condition. In this sense, putafeminism repurposes the Black feminist call to center the most vulnerable among us; as Margo St. James argued, “the word whore is used to stigmatize any woman that doesn’t fit the criteria of a good girl.” If whores themselves refuse to be daunted by stigma and shame, then perhaps we can collectively chip away at the forces that too often make sex unfulfilling and perilous for all women, forces that make rape, femicide, slut-shaming, and revenge porn all too common. To take a “whore’s-eye view” on questions of desire, power, and human frailty is to discover a feminism in which “no one loses,” Prada writes. “On the contrary, we all win.”

entries.title: ‘The Silent Art’
entries.summary: Kate Millett would never be more active or more in demand than she was in 1972. Two summers earlier, her debut book had made her a household name. entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Kate Millett would never be more active or more in demand than she was in 1972. Two summers earlier, her debut book had made her a household name. Begun as her thesis for a literature Ph.D., Sexual Politics swelled into a wide-ranging examination of sex as a terrain of political contest and patriarchy as a ubiquitous force, adaptable but tenacious throughout history, structuring interpersonal life at every scale. The press seized on the book as an exemplary artifact of a new wave of feminism striking the shores of the mainstream.

After Time put her portrait on its cover and dubbed her “the Mao Tse-tung of Women’s Liberation,” Millett struggled to wrench the spotlight back toward the causes she’d been made to represent. She spoke at rallies, college auditoriums, and closed-door rap sessions. She appeared on Dick Cavett and on the steps of the New York capitol. In March 1972 she returned to Columbia, where she’d been a graduate student, to protest layoffs of custodial staff; in May she traveled to California to witness the trial of Angela Davis. And in April she mounted an art show called Terminal Piece.

Millett had been making art for over a decade, a parallel vocation that was met with mild curiosity when it was acknowledged at all. A spread in Life introduced her as a “furious young philosopher” before noting that she was also “a sometime artist” of “whimsical sculpture.” An accompanying photo shows her smiling broadly behind one of her creations: a cartoonish wooden bed with four oversized feet stretching out toward the camera. It was one of a suite of furniture pieces that brought Millett modest attention in the late 1960s, before the press reencountered her on the barricades. “Kate Millett’s sculptures all look alike and like Kate Millett,” Janet Malcolm wrote in The New Yorker. “They have a square-cut, blocky, strong, optimistic character.”

Terminal Piece was something else. No one would call it whimsical or optimistic. Millett’s installation has been restaged this summer at mumok, in Vienna, where it occupies its own shadowy room on the museum’s top floor. A wall of wooden bars cuts the space in two. Behind them are arranged two rows of folding chairs. A single mannequin sits off-center in the second row, her head bowed slightly, her right foot arched forward. She wears the loose navy dress of a prisoner, penitent, or sleeper, and incongruous black high heels. She may be waiting to stand and depart (terminal as in transit stop), or she may be waiting forever (terminal as in fatal).

It’s a disturbingly lonely work, especially from an artist who did not want for company. The 1972 opening at the Women’s Interart Center, a feminist gallery on 52nd Street in Manhattan, was packed with well-wishers. Writing in Ms., Millett’s friend Bertha Harris described the evening as a raucous party from which only the mannequin was excluded: “In the middle of our noise, she is a stillness like embalmed death.” Harris longed to free the woman from her cage, and as the night wore on some revelers finally did. Millett later remembered watching as her mannequin was swallowed by the crowd, “a rigid figure who could neither drink nor converse while they chattered and milled about.”

For months she had felt herself grow rigid, embalmed in her own celebrity. “I can’t be Kate Millett anymore,” she confessed in Flying (1974), a memoir of her effort to transcend her figurehead status. “It’s an object, a thing. A joke at cocktail parties.” When, she must have wondered, would someone liberate her?

It still surprises people to learn that Millett, who died in 2017, made sculptures, but a string of posthumous exhibitions has stoked new interest in them. Terminal Piece was previously revived at Bard College’s Hessel Museum in 2021. Later that year, the Dorsky at SUNY New Paltz mounted “Life After the Revolution,” a group show about the art colony run by Millett and her partner Sophie Keir on Millett’s Dutchess County farm beginning in the late 1970s. More attention was garnered by “Fantasy Furniture, 1967” at Salon 94 Design, which featured the furniture works made just before Millett was pushed onto the national stage.

Eerily animate, these pieces both invite and repel use. A 1967 photo shows Millett seated on Uncle Louis Stool with Boots, her back to the camera, her lower half obscured by the sculpture in a visual gag: its slender wooden legs are painted with striped stockings and wear oversized work shoes. Bachelor’s Apartment has a squat head made from a milliner’s hat block, blank but for a pair of wide blue eyes angled slightly to one side, puzzled and expectant. In place of its torso is a cupboard stocked with dishware; a wooden hand seems to hold one door open like a flasher’s trench coat.

Advertisement

For viewers who know Millett only as a firebrand, her furniture can be a revelation: clever and charming, but odd; in touch with the avant-gardes of its own moment, but as alive half a century later as it must have been when first shown in a basement gallery at Judson Memorial Church. Millett had lived in Japan at the start of the 1960s, where she fell in with a bohemian set of artists and poets more influenced by surrealism, Dada, and Duchamp than by the abstract expressionism that dominated in New York. Upon her return to the US, Millett—like many of her friends, including Yoko Ono and Carolee Schneemann—found an aesthetic home on the outskirts of Fluxus, a loose international movement that (in the words of its ringleader, George Maciunas) opposed “the separation of art and life.”

Much Fluxus work was self-consciously political. Maciunas imagined that by stripping art of its pretensions and exclusivity, Fluxus would “purge the world of bourgeois sickness.” Millett’s furniture was political, too, in the sense that Sexual Politics helped popularize: the sculptures concern “power-structured relationships” as they play out in the close quarters of home. Their ambivalently innocent and ominous tone speaks to the tenderness as well as the alienation of domestic life, its pleasures as well as its indignities. The two humanoid forms in Bed seem to stare vacantly at the ceiling. They aren’t touching; a break in the mattress ticking with which the piece is upholstered gives their double bed the look of twin beds pushed together, or coffins laid side by side. The conjoined chairs of Love Seat face in opposite directions, and the figures that occupy them likewise look past and away from each other.

Reviews of Salon 94 Design’s 2022 show tended to underline this incipient feminist critique while still describing the furniture as a buoyant relic of Millett’s not-yet-raised consciousness, a prologue to her activist career. That was, in fact, how Millett herself came to see it. In a 1988 essay for Art Papers, she wrote that her mid-Sixties sculptures were made “out of a happiness with form itself…intent upon ingenuity, a Mozartian wit and grace. I had a wonderful time.”

In her own telling, her approach changed overnight when, in 1966, she read a magazine article about the abuse and murder of an Indiana teenager named Sylvia Likens. Likens’s guardian enlisted her own children and neighbors in torturing the girl, who was confined to a basement for weeks before her death. The phrase I AM A PROSTITUTE AND PROUD OF IT was etched across her stomach.

Likens’s story struck Millett as “a devastation of the spirit like the collapse of a building.” It fueled the writing of Sexual Politics and gave her the image that defined her art for the next decade, including Terminal Piece: the cage. In the summer of 1967—the Summer of Love, for some—Millett spent six weeks constructing a maze of wooden walls and dowels in the basement of her Bowery building and filling it with dismembered mannequins. This installation, called Trap, was followed by the performance No, for which unsuspecting visitors were imprisoned within a structure Millett built inside Judson’s basement gallery. (The art critic Lil Picard, who was running late for a TV appearance, organized the crowd’s escape.) Situations, installed in 1968 at a community college in downtown Brooklyn, used Millett’s new motif to recast her earlier work. Pieces of furniture, now stripped of whimsy, were displayed in cages in the college’s courtyard: “the domestic safety of a dining room table” at once “exposed” and “enclosed in bars.”

Likens’s murder clearly had a profound effect on Millett; her 1979 book The Basement, which recounts the crime in horrible detail, attests to its enduring imprint on her thinking. But this conversion narrative neutralizes the bite of Millett’s furniture, some of which was made after she first read about Likens, and it threatens to clip the associative power of the work that followed. Even as the cage symbolized the extremity of women’s subjection, it also suggested links between misogyny and other kinds of “confinement,” as she wrote in Art Papers:

the torment of being someone’s amusement, someone’s job in that they are employed to torment you. Who are the food of guards and watchmen, their bland indifferent eyes. The captured, pawns of the state, of faceless government, disinterested army personnel, attendants of “corrections” or the “mental health system.”

Likens was “there in the shadows” of Trap alongside a row of urinals flanked by papier-mâché legs, meant to evoke US soldiers’ sexual exploitation of Vietnamese women. Perhaps Millett’s most infamous cage appeared in the 1970 People’s Flag Show at Judson, intended to challenge flag desecration laws that had been wielded against antiwar activists. Her contribution, The American Dream Goes to Pot, consisted of a toilet bowl detained in a wooden cell. The stars and stripes were draped over the bowl’s lip—to be flushed down the drain, presumably, though it always puts me in mind of some sewer creature crawling up through the pipes.

Advertisement

In this light the mannequin of Terminal Piece conjures what Millett called “the lone Giacometti-like stick of a citizen reduced to a number, a cell, a punch card, a clinical or criminal history.” While making it she read Solzhenitsyn on the Gulags and began to advocate for political prisoners; in subsequent months she would publish two long essays about Angela Davis in Ms. and teach a course on “Prisons and the Prison Movement.” At the same time, Terminal Piece is sparer and more ambiguous than its sibling works. It picks up their political concerns and knits them in turn to the artist’s inner turmoil, which was, in 1972, still mostly private.

To Janet Malcolm, whose New Yorker story published just weeks before Terminal Piece opened, Millett confessed her “puritanism about work” and the joylessness of her effort to keep art alive amid the media circus. Her husband Fumio Yoshimura, also a sculptor, told Malcolm that Sexual Politics “destroyed our quiet life.” Though their content was grim, her earlier cage pieces had channeled a certain hopefulness in both Fluxus and the women’s movement. By demanding their audiences’ active engagement, Trap and No took for granted that people can be moved to change their circumstances, and that art and ideas can spur that change. The inert mannequin of Terminal Piece may admit some disillusionment with that dream. In a short item in Parade, Millett said elliptically, “I feel an identification with the loneliness and despair of the figure because it’s a place I’ve been.” She had a history of depressions and would soon show signs of mania, for which she was hospitalized in 1973. The ordeal led her to see herself as one of “the underground people.” The asylum was part of the continuum of imprisonment that already preoccupied her work and defined her century.

Millett’s 1974 book Flying describes her struggle against celebrity and the fraying of her marriage, but it took her years to write about her time in institutions, just as it took years to write about Likens. In the meantime she made sculpture, which she once called “the silent art.” Her cages gave form to the prisons of fame, of psychiatry, of sex, and their “obdurate tangibility” provided a measure of relief from the vaporous meanings that clung to her.

Terminal Piece is too solid and too oblique to symbolize any one thing. At mumok, it anchors an ambitious show featuring dozens of artists across five of the museum’s floors, suggesting new links and associations. In lieu of biographical or historical through lines, the curators, Fatima Hellberg and Lukas Flygare, highlight the power dynamics that shape the act of looking itself: What does it mean to stand on the viewer’s side of the frame? On the artist’s? These questions helped me see that Terminal Piece is participatory in its own way. Millett’s mannequin might be an audience of one for the show that we make; as the exhibition program suggests, “It becomes unclear who exactly is being put on view.” (Millett once named Ionesco’s The Chairs and Beckett’s Waiting for Godot among her inspirations for the work.)

mumok’s galleries are full of obstructed sightlines and partial barriers to peek over or around. Mirrors, windows, and doorways recur, sometimes opening onto nothing. Many of the displayed artworks—like Kobby Adi’s The Machine (2026), in which a bioimaging device has been refitted to transmit live black-and-white footage to screens throughout the gallery—riff on surveillance and the conventions of documentary. Many appropriate mundane objects and make them strange. The show’s great discovery, for me, was probably Louis Goodman’s winning assemblages of forks, springs, jewelry, and other household odds and ends, from 1964—the same moment in which Millett was making her fantasy furniture.

And many of these artists share Millett’s interest in the intimate scale at which vast social forces mark our lives. In the years after Sexual Politics, as she strained to incorporate ever more causes into her feminism, she also worked to refocus it on what she described (quoting Thoreau) as “the quiet desperation” of the individual. This was evident in the writing for which she’s best known—the scholarly voice of her first book was soon supplanted by a nervy and vulnerable first person—and it was evident in sculptures like Terminal Piece. One thing the cage said to Millett was that each of us suffers alone. Yet she never stopped believing that suffering could be a basis for solidarity. There is a certain “responsibility these symbols confer upon us,” she wrote about her solitary sculptural figures in Art Papers. “There is no Sadean glorification of anguish at issue, no sentimental gloating over wretchedness—they are there to be liberated.”

entries.title: Jerry Survives
entries.summary: As an artist in the second half of the twentieth century, Jerry Moriarty did everything you weren’t supposed to do: he painted people, he painted places, and, perhaps worst of all, he told stories with pictures. entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
As an artist in the second half of the twentieth century, Jerry Moriarty did everything you weren’t supposed to do: he painted people, he painted places, and, perhaps worst of all, he told stories with pictures. It’s important to note how not-accepted this was between the 1950s and 1970s, in the messy aftermath of abstract expressionism, when many artists had disowned figuration and family in favor of non-objective paint-spattered flats. But Jerry drew pictures of America as Americans remembered it, if not even still lived it: childhood, parents, home. Like many of his peers, he spent much of his career alone in a small Manhattan studio but, upon retirement, he moved back to his childhood home.

Like many people, I was first introduced to Jerry’s work in the pages of Art Spiegelman and Françoise Mouly’s RAW magazine via his strip Jack Survives, in which the eponymous character, both Jerry’s dad yet also not his dad, passed quick, quiet moments of the everyday. Jerry’s bold, solid, black-and-white strips seemed to have been pencilled by Ernie Bushmiller and inked by Edward Hopper, proffering a loud-but-soft view of middle-class midcentury America. Like so much in RAW, it felt strange, but unlike so much in RAW, it also felt strangely familiar. Jerry’s strips somehow caught the scent of sun-warmed houses and 1940s sofas and made the time when men wore hats and women wore housedresses feel real. A window into what I’d imagined my grandparents’ early lives might’ve been like, his work chided the squareness of that generation but with a gentle empathy for their difficulties (war, economic scrimping), without the dismissiveness that some baby-boomer writers and artists seemed to have for their parents. His bold, sturdily composed panels and solid sense of objects and people lent it an eternal quality, seemingly in conflict with the ineffability of its domestic situations and the dissipating half-life of conversations, thoughts,

and the words one says only when talking to oneself, the whole adding up to not exactly a comic strip, but something like a picture-poem with a punchline.

The first collection of Jack Survives, published in 1984 by RAW Books and Graphics, was designed by Spiegelman and Mouly, its cover separating Jerry’s eight-crayon-box colors and his bold black brush drawing into two layers, the ink lines printed on an acetate jacket which under one’s fingers slipped in and out of alignment with the bright hues below. It reminded me of the anatomy overlays in my grandparents’ encyclopedias, and offered a lesson in not only how comics were printed but also the basic cognitive distinction between drawing and painting (to say nothing of the difference between remembering something and actually seeing it). His original comics pages are strange palimpsests, in which penciled memory-details disappear under acrylic white or emerge as emphasized ink, the approach more evident in the 2008 reprint of Jack Survives, in which Jerry chose to highlight his pages’ simultaneous boldness and delicacy in full-color scans instead of the contrasting black-and-white of the first edition. In a way, this echoed his overall artistic method: Jerry’s assertive, Hopper-esque drawings—see Hopper’s etchings, especially—mellowed once they made it into his paintings, softening into full-color acrylic studies on paper before ending with his almost diaphanous oils on canvas. These paintings, generally composed of three, sometimes four brightly colored panels, were meant to be not just looked at, but read.

Jerry wanted to be accessible and eschewed pretension, later labeling himself a “paintoonist” as a sort of self-effacing and disarming pre-strike against anyone who might consider denigrating his efforts, for which he was always on high alert. In his early life he’d tried abstraction and also working as an illustrator, but found he was comfortable with neither, disappearing into a private life subsidized by working as a teacher at the School of Visual Arts in New York. Over a period of several decades he produced a considerable oeuvre that basically no one ever saw unless they visited his Manhattan studio/loft.

As I tried to become a thoughtful cartoonist myself, Jack Survives was never far from my mind, frequently open on my drawing table at moments of desperation, where I’d reread his strips several dozen times while avoiding my own. Eventually, I got to meet Jerry in person, the first time at a 2004 exhibit of his paintings in Manhattan which Spiegelman had organized. I’d thoroughly expected to shake the hand of a dour, literary Thornton Wilder in a houndstooth jacket and trim tie, but instead was met by a spritely, energetic marionette in bright orange pants who seemed to leap between his canvases, weightless long white hair trailing a beat behind him as he narrated the backstory to each one, the paintings’ fictional characters melding with his experience of making them.

Advertisement

At that point in his career he’d been drawing and painting “Sally,” a character who was a sort of authorial stand-in (again, partly him yet really not him) and about whom he spoke from the inside (“Sally wanted to climb the tree”) and the outside (“I felt so wrong painting that”)—and, most importantly, with real affection. None of the paintings were for sale. He made his work only for himself, amassing it slowly and, as he later described it to me, working in the “art protection business” to make sure that nothing ever escaped, except the very few pieces he offered as gifts. Neither a gallery-affiliated fine artist nor a job-hungry commercial artist, he had more or less committed career suicide, leaving such possible-life husks behind so he could float above them, living purely through, and for, his work.

The second time I met Jerry was at a party in 2007 at Spiegelman and Mouly’s apartment, with other RAW cartoonists in attendance, Kim Deitch and Charles Burns and Gary Panter among many more. I ended up talking to Jerry alone for what must’ve been almost an hour, he at one point going into great detail about how he lived off a whole pre-cooked grocery store chicken and six chocolate chip cookies per week, carefully apportioning them over seven days to keep himself and his cat alive. He offered this not as a look-at-me-I’m-crazy detail but as what we’d now call a “life hack.” During this hour in his presence a very tangible sense of aloneness enveloped me. I mention this not to embarrass his memory, but to clarify: as Jerry said in an interview I did with him for The Believer in 2009, “I am a loner, and I fully understand why that makes me strange to society … but I am not lonely. Being alone is total freedom for me.”

Put another way, his memories were his company. This is indeed just the sort of person who would discover his childhood home was for sale, buy it, and move back in. There, he set up his studio in the very basement where he’d made art as a kid and where his dad would arrive home from work to sit and talk with him as he drew and painted. Now in his seventies, Jerry started drawing and painting images of his father and his mother at the ages they were when he was a child, but with himself pictured as the old man he had become. In one painting, Jerry’s head peeps through a rip in the paper ceiling above his father, who sits in an easy chair below; in another, old Jerry sits at the kitchen table talking to his young mother, easily half his age. (My stepfather, now living alone following the death of my mother in May, told me that every night he sits in his armchair and tells her what’s happened over the course of the day.) These were the people and memories that meant the most to Jerry—his parents, his siblings, his childhood dog. (When he was a kid, his dog had been taken away by the humane society, a loss for which Jerry offers a painted corrective: the dog returns to the front door, where a child-sized old-man Jerry lets him in, then spends the night on the floor, cradling him.)

These are not the traditional tropes of comics, but of literature and poetry. My favorites of Jerry’s works get at those moments when we completely surrender, when we’re at our most vulnerable—exactly the opposite of what comics’ brash denigration and guffaws generally paper over. His tenderness, when it’s the focus, is without precedent in cartooning—or, for that matter, in much contemporary art. And that Jerry managed it all within such a “loud,” disreputable language as comics is especially remarkable. He was the first cartoonist to realize that by leaning into the loud, like his cartoonist hero Bushmiller, one might be able to more closely approach the quiet of real life. It’s one of the mysteries of comics, hiding somewhere between the giant/infinitesimal horror of a childhood fever and the lyrical dissonance of the bebop jazz that Jerry loved (and played).*

Advertisement

Jerry thought and drew (though what’s the difference?) a lot about death. It is the implicit theme in his late work Whatsa Paintoonist?—which is also one of the weirdest titles for one of the greatest graphic novels ever. This is the book that collects his imagined revisitations with his parents, painted in the home where they all once lived, and in which, through his drawings, Jerry says his goodbyes to them. It is also the home where, in March of this year, Jerry’s nephew found him dead. The book resuscitates the childhood feeling that most of us spend our lives tamping down and dismissing, if not completely extinguishing. It’s a magical, alchemical experience of reading and seeing, somehow mixing Jerry’s own memories of childhood and parents with one’s own, on the page and in the mind’s eye. It reawakens some sleeping small self within us, completely disarmingly and without pretension. It captures the feeling of life, but most especially, of love.
